'''David Horn''' ({{Langx|he|דוד הורן}}; born 10 September 1937) is a [[Professor]] (Emeritus) of [[Physics]] in the School of Physics and [[Astronomy]] at [[Tel Aviv University]] (TAU), [[Israel]]. He has served as Vice-[[Rector (academia)|Rector]] of TAU, Chairman of the School of Physics and Astronomy and as [[Dean (education)|Dean]] of the Faculty of [[Exact Sciences]] in TAU.<ref name=cv>{{citation|title=David Horn – CV|url=http://horn.tau.ac.il/about.html|publisher=Tel Aviv University|date= 2019}}</ref> He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, nominated for "contributions to theoretical particle physics, including the seminal work on finite energy sum rules, research of the phenomenology of hadronic processes, and investigation of [[Hamiltonian lattice gauge theory|Hamiltonian lattice theories]]".<ref name=APS>{{citation|title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1985&unit_id=DPF&institution=Tel+Aviv+University |publisher=[[American Physical Society]]}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
David Horn was born and educated in [[Haifa]]. He graduated from the [[Reali School]] in 1955. He began his academic studies in Physics at the [[Technion]] in Haifa in 1957, and received his B.Sc. (Summa Cum Laude) in 1961, and M.Sc. in 1962. He continued his Ph.D. studies at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]] until 1965. His thesis on "Some Aspects of the Structure of Weak Interactions" was supervised by Prof. [[Yuval Ne'eman]].<ref name=cv/>

==Career==
Horn joined the newly founded Tel Aviv University as an assistant in 1962. He became a lecturer in 1965, a senior lecturer in 1967 and an associate professor in 1968. He was promoted to full professor of Physics in 1972. In 1974 he became the incumbent of the Edouard and Francoise Jaupart Chair of Theoretical Physics of Particles and Fields, a position he held until 2007. Horn has supervised 43 graduate students at TAU and authored over 240 scientific publications.<ref name=cv/> He retired as a professor emeritus in 2005, and continues to be an active researcher.<ref name=google_scholar>{{citation|title=David Horn (sorted by publication date)|url=https://scholar.google.co.il/citations?hl=en&user=gjKDpHIAAAAJ&view_op=list_works&sortby=pubdate|publisher=[[Google Scholar]]|date= 2020}}</ref>

Horn spent a significant part of his career holding visiting academic positions at other universities and research institutes, including:  Postdoctoral Fellow at [[Argonne National Lab]], ILL, Research Fellow and three times Visiting Associate at [[California Institute of Technology]], [[Pasadena]], CA, Visitor at [[CERN]] in [[Geneva]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Horn |first=D. |year=1972 |title=Many-particle production |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/037015737290021X |journal=Physics Reports |language=en |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=1–65 |doi=10.1016/0370-1573(72)90021-X|bibcode=1972PhR.....4....1H |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Visiting Professor at [[Cornell University]], NY, Member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], [[Princeton, NJ]],<ref>{{citation|title=David Horn |date=9 December 2019 |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/david-horn|publisher= The Institute for Advanced Study}}</ref>  Visiting Professor at [[SLAC]] in [[Stanford University]], CA, and Visiting Professor at [[Kyoto University]], [[Japan]].

Beginning from 1980, Horn held official positions at Tel Aviv University, starting with tenure as Vice-Rector (1980-1983),<ref>{{citation|title=Prof. David Horn - Vice-Rector of TAU (in Hebrew) |url=http://www.jpress.nli.org.il/Olive/APA/NLI_heb/SharedView.Article.aspx?href=MAR%2F1980%2F09%2F01&id=Ar00406&sk=65BFDF93|publisher=[[Maariv (newspaper)|Maariv]]|date=1980}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Past Leadership of Tel Aviv University |date=18 November 2012 |url=https://english.m.tau.ac.il/past_leadership|publisher=Tel Aviv University}}</ref> a position he left for research at SLAC. After returning he was nominated Chairman of the Department of High Energy Physics (1984-1986), followed by tenures as Chairman of the School of Physics and Astronomy (1986-9),<ref>{{citation|title=History of the School |url=https://physics.tau.ac.il/shcool_history|publisher=Tel Aviv University}}</ref>  Dean of the Raymond and Beverly Sackler Faculty of Exact Sciences (1990-1995), and first Director of the Adams Super Center for Brain Studies (1993-2000).<ref name=cv/>

Horn has also held national and international professional positions. He was Chairman of the Israel Commission for [[High Energy Physics]] (1983-2003), and, in this capacity, served as an Israeli observer of the council of CERN (1991-2003).<ref>{{citation|title=CERN and Israel |url=https://inis.iaea.org/collection/NCLCollectionStore/_Public/47/127/47127203.pdf?r=1&r=1|publisher=[[CERN Courier]]|date=1995| volume=35 | issue=4 | pages=24–27 }}</ref>
He served as member of the [[Israel Council for Higher Education]] (1987-1991), member of the Executive Committee of the [[European Physical Society]] (1989-1992) and member of the European Strategy Forum on Research Infrastructures (2005-2017). He chaired the Israeli Committee of Research Infrastructures (2012-2016), issuing roadmaps for scientific RI in 2013 and 2016.<ref name=cv/>

==Research==
Horn's research work focused on theory and phenomenology of High Energy Physics until 1990. He then shifted his interests to [[Neural Computation]] and [[Machine Learning]] and, since 2005, he has also published in [[Bioinformatics]].<ref name=google_scholar/>

Together with Richard Dolen and Christoph Schmid he discovered the [[History of string theory|Finite Energy Sum Rules]] in 1967. It was a realization of the bootstrap approach to hadronic structure, and became known as the [[String theory|Dolen-Horn-Schmid Duality]].<ref name="IPS">{{citation|last=|first=|title=IPS Fellows 2018|url=https://www.israelphysicalsociety.org/ips-conference-2018/ips-fellows|volume=|pages=|publisher=The Israel Physical Society|access-date=25 January 2021|archive-date=1 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210201115728/https://www.israelphysicalsociety.org/ips-conference-2018/ips-fellows}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Dolen-Horn-Schmid Duality and the Deck Effect|publisher=[[Physical Review Letters]] D|date=1968|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.20.1078|last1=Chew|first1=G. F.|last2=Pignotti|first2=A.|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=20|issue=19|pages=1078–1081|bibcode=1968PhRvL..20.1078C}}</ref>

Together with Richard Silver he investigated a model of coherent production of [[pions]] at high energy [[hadron]] collisions in 1971,<ref>{{citation|title=Coherent production of pions|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/352335/files/CM-P00058697.pdf|publisher=[[Annals of Physics]]|date=1971}}</ref>
and  together with [[Jeffrey Mandula]] he undertook the investigation of [[meson]]s with constituent [[gluons]] in 1978.<ref>{{citation|title=Model of mesons with constituent gluons |journal=Physical Review D|date=1978|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.17.898|last1=Horn|first1=D.|last2=Mandula|first2=J.|volume=17|issue=3|pages=898–908|bibcode=1978PhRvD..17..898H|url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:HORprd78 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
Moving to [[Lattice gauge theory|lattice gauge theories]] in 1979, he discovered,  together with Shimon Yankielowic and Marvin Weinstein, a non-confining phase in Z(N) theories for large N.<ref>{{citation|title=Hamiltonian approach to Z(N) lattice gauge theories|journal=Physical Review D|date=1979|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.19.3715|last1=Horn|first1=D.|last2=Weinstein|first2=M.|last3=Yankielowicz|first3=S.|volume=19|issue=12|pages=3715–3731|bibcode=1979PhRvD..19.3715H}}</ref>
In 1981 he demonstrated the existence of finite matrix models with link gauge fields,<ref>{{citation|title=Finite matrix models with continuous local gauge invariance|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0370269381907632|journal=[[Physics Letters B]]|date=1981|bibcode=1981PhLB..100..149H|last1=Horn|first1=D.|volume=100|issue=2|page=149|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(81)90763-2|url-access=subscription}}</ref> nowadays known as quantum link models.<ref>{{citation|title=Quantum Link Models: A Discrete Approach to Gauge Theories|publisher=[[MIT]]|date=2008|doi=10.1016/S0550-3213(97)80041-7|arxiv=hep-lat/9609042|last1=Chandrasekharan|first1=S.|last2=Wiese|first2=U.-J|journal=Nuclear Physics B|volume=492|issue=1–2|pages=455–471|s2cid=8718204}}</ref>
In 1984 Horn and Weinstein developed the t-expansion methodology.<ref>{{citation|title=The t expansion: A nonperturbative analytic tool for Hamiltonian systems|journal=Physical Review D|date=1984|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.30.1256|last1=Horn|first1=D.|last2=Weinstein|first2=M.|volume=30|issue=6|pages=1256–1270|bibcode=1984PhRvD..30.1256H}}</ref>

Horn's contributions to neural modeling include a novel mechanism for memory maintenance via neuronal regulation in 1998, developed with Nir Levy and Eytan Ruppin<ref>{{citation|title=Memory Maintenance via Neuronal Regulation|journal=[[Neural Computation (journal)|Neural Computation]]|date=1998|doi=10.1162/089976698300017863|last1=Horn|first1=David|last2=Levy|first2=Nir|last3=Ruppin|first3=Eytan|volume=10|issue=1|pages=1–18|pmid=9501502|s2cid=1453974}}</ref>
and unsupervised learning of [[Natural language processing|natural languages]] in 2005, a joint work with Zach Solan, Eytan Ruppin and Shimon Edelman,<ref>{{citation|title=Unsupervised learning of natural languages |publisher=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]]|date=2005|doi=10.1073/pnas.0409746102 |doi-access=free |last1=Solan |first1=Zach |last2=Horn |first2=David |last3=Ruppin |first3=Eytan |last4=Edelman |first4=Shimon |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=102 |issue=33 |pages=11629–11634 |pmid=16087885 |pmc=1187953 |bibcode=2005PNAS..10211629S }}</ref> introducing novel [[algorithm]]s for motif and grammar extraction from text. Horn has contributed to algorithms of clustering, an important topic in Machine Learning, by developing [[Support vector machine|Support Vector Clustering]] (SVC) in 2001,<ref>{{citation|title=Support Vector Clustering|url=https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/papers/volume2/horn01a/horn01a.pdf|publisher=[[Journal of Machine Learning Research]]|date=2001}}</ref> together with Asa Ben Hur, [[Hava Siegelmann]] and Vladimir Vapnik. This was followed shortly thereafter by a joint work with Assaf Gottlieb on [[Quantum clustering|Quantum Clustering]] (QC).<ref>{{citation|title=Algorithm for Data Clustering in Pattern Recognition Problems Based on Quantum Mechanics |journal=Physical Review Letters|date=2001|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.88.018702|last1=Horn|first1=David|last2=Gottlieb|first2=Assaf|volume=88|issue=1|article-number=018702|pmid=11800996|bibcode=2001PhRvL..88a8702H |arxiv=physics/0107063}}</ref>
 
His contributions to Bioinformatics include motif descriptions of function and structure of [[protein]]s,  as well as motif studies of genomic structures. Together with Erez Persi he studied compositional order of [[proteomes]],  and repeat instability of genomes, as evolution markers of organisms<ref>{{citation|title=Systematic Analysis of Compositional Order of Proteins Reveals New Characteristics of Biological Functions and a Universal Correlate of Macroevolution |journal=PLOS Computational Biology|date=2013|doi = 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003346|last1 = Persi|first1 = Erez|last2 = Horn|first2 = David|volume = 9|issue = 11|article-number = e1003346|pmid = 24278003|pmc=3836704|bibcode = 2013PLSCB...9E3346P|s2cid = 8454460 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and of [[cancer]] (a joint work with Persi and others).<ref>{{citation|title=Proteomic and genomic signatures of repeat instability in cancer and adjacent normal tissues |publisher=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|date=2019|bibcode=2019PNAS..11616987P |last1=Persi |first1=Erez |last2=Prandi |first2=Davide |last3=Wolf |first3=Yuri I. |last4=Pozniak |first4=Yair |last5=Barnabas |first5=Georgina D. |last6=Levanon |first6=Keren |last7=Barshack |first7=Iris |last8=Barbieri |first8=Christopher |last9=Gasperini |first9=Paola |last10=Beltran |first10=Himisha |last11=Faltas |first11=Bishoy M. |last12=Rubin |first12=Mark A. |last13=Geiger |first13=Tamar |last14=Koonin |first14=Eugene V. |last15=Demichelis |first15=Francesca |last16=Horn |first16=David |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=116 |issue=34 |pages=16987–16996 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1908790116 |pmid=31387980 |pmc=6708321 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Honors==
Horn is a Fellow of the American Physical Society (1985)<ref name=APS/> and a Fellow of the Israel Physical Society (2018).<ref name=IPS/>

==Personal life==
Horn was married to Nira Fuss since 1963 until her death in 2019. He is a father of three, Yuval, Tamar, and Oded, and grandfather of nine. He lives in [[Tel Aviv]], Israel.
